source.title: Generalized Federated Learning via Sharpness Aware Minimization
source.authors: Zhe Qu; Xingyu Li; Rui Duan; Yaojiang Liu; Bo Tang; Zhuo Lu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations, tables, and figure text are visibly flattened or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: Compares FedSAM/MoFedSAM with federated learning benchmarks on training and validation accuracy, and measures loss-surface sharpness. These are conceptual tests of optimizer-related generalization and sharpness, in a heterogeneous federated setting.
record.gate_note: Results on federated training versus validation performance and loss-surface sharpness bear on V4 and V7. No random-label memorization, width sweep, architecture comparison, batch-size comparison, dropout intervention, or memorized-example removal is tested. Values used only in figures without stated numerical outcomes are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima improve generalization to develop federated SAM algorithms and evaluates their performance. It does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD or test whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks generalization gaps. Its results therefore test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate but overstates unrestricted outperformance. The authors conclude that FedSAM and MoFedSAM improve global-model generalization and reduce performance variation across clients, supported by convergence analysis and a FedSAM generalization bound. Their empirical superiority claims compare algorithms within the same momentum category; FedSAM does not outperform the momentum baselines.
record.recipe_differences: Federated learning with non-IID client distributions; tests local SAM and momentum FedSAM against federated benchmarks, not the centralized optimizer, batch-size, architecture, or sharpness-measurement recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and client-distribution heterogeneity affect accuracy; the paper reports different outcomes across datasets and IID/Dirichlet settings. SAM perturbation radius and momentum parameter are varied, but numeric figure values are not extracted.

fits_no_version.finding: FedSAM improves validation accuracy over FedAvg from 81.87% to 83.06% on CIFAR-10, 53.57% to 54.69% on CIFAR-100, and 84.38% to 84.75% on EMNIST under the default heterogeneous federated setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Using SAM for local optimization can improve held-out accuracy relative to FedAvg in heterogeneous federated learning.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors qualitatively describe FedSAM and MoFedSAM loss surfaces as flatter than FedAvg for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Federated SAM algorithms can produce flatter plotted loss surfaces than FedAvg along sampled perturbation directions.

record.problems: The study is in federated non-IID settings, so its results do not directly establish the centralized generalization claims. Figure 2 sharpness evidence is qualitative, and numerical table results report standard deviations but do not isolate optimizer choice from all other federated algorithm differences.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows kept from figures whose plotted values are not stated numerically in text. Figures 1, 3–6 and Tables 2, 4, 5 report additional algorithm, heterogeneity, or parameter conditions, but the extracted table rows cover the principal SAM-versus-FedAvg results and loss-surface comparison; the remaining separately reported numeric conditions were omitted for focus.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning-budget dependence and recovery strategies.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. The passing statement about batch size supplies no such comparison.
Effects of adding or removing dropout. Including dropout in the EMNIST architecture is not an intervention.

Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. The theoretical bound and qualitative loss surfaces do not test these relationships.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed limits_scope verdicts: failure to measure a version is an untested component, not evidence limiting it. The extracted Table 1 means are accurate, although some appendix values conflict with the main table. Omitted federated benchmark results do not require missing entries because they bear on none of the supplied versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
No network-width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers such as Adam against SGD; compares federated algorithms using SAM and ERM-based local optimization.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No dropout intervention or dropout configuration comparison.
Sharpness is visualized as loss surfaces for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10; no magnitude-aware weight perturbations or comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining.

rows.subject: FedAvg
rows.operation_detail: FedAvg federated training; table reports mean training and validation accuracy across clients.
rows.note: ERM-based federated benchmark; no adaptive optimizer comparison.
rows.check: Table 1 values are correct, but FedAvg is a federated algorithm comparator, not an adaptive-versus-SGD comparison. This is a method-performance row outside the claim versions.

rows.subject: FedSAM
rows.operation_detail: FedSAM with SAM local optimizer; table reports mean training and validation accuracy across clients.
rows.note: Compared with FedAvg, both reported accuracies are higher; this is a federated SAM-versus-ERM comparison, not an adaptive-optimizer test.
rows.check: Values and baseline match Table 1. SAM versus FedAvg does not measure V4; higher validation accuracy cannot establish a partial adaptive-optimizer effect.

rows.subject: FedSAM

rows.subject: FedAvg
rows.operation_detail: Loss-surface visualization using two random sampled orthogonal Gaussian perturbations.
rows.value: Figure-only visualization; authors state its loss surface is sharper than FedSAM and MoFedSAM.
rows.note: Authors describe both SAM methods as improving sharpness significantly in comparison to FedAvg.
rows.check: The qualitative Gaussian-direction loss-surface visualization does not establish magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps. Figure 2 is the correct figure; Section 5.2(3) mistakenly refers to Figure 3.

rows.check: The authors describe a flatter loss surface, but report no magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or gap-ranking analysis. This cannot be coded as a partial V7 effect.
